pending_commit.commit_message: CHROMIUM: alt-syscall: add sysctl entry to allow dev mode-only syscalls Chromium OS defines a few alt-syscall tables to whitelist certain system calls in a container. There are scenarios when we would like to expose more system calls to a container, but only do so when the host system is in the developer mode. To allow that, this CL adds a sysctl entry 'kernel/chromiumos/alt_syscall/allow_devmode_syscalls', which can be controlled by a privileged system service. The system service decides whether developer mode-only system calls are allowed by performing checks on the current mode and any applied device policies (see CL:421087 and CL:425454) BUG=b:33450588 TEST=Verify that the added sysctl entry '/proc/sys/kernel/chromiumos/alt_syscall/allow_devmode_syscalls' exists and can only be written by root. Change-Id: Id7c61b8c13de22c5b0f70b3ebb165e35418d28a2 Signed-off-by: Ben Chan <benchan@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/425861 Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>

CHROMIUM: alt-syscall: whitelist perf_event_open for Android Android provides a native profiling tool called simpleperf, which uses the perf_event_open system call exposed by the Linux kernel. Android CTS has a CtsSimpleperfTestCases module that tests various simpleperf usage. To allow simpleperf and CtsSimpleperfTestCases running under the Android container on ChromeOS, this CL whitelists the perf_event_open system call in the alt-syscall table for Android only when we allow developer mode-only system calls, which is controlled by the `kernel/chromiumos/alt_syscall/allow_devmode_syscalls` sysctl entry. BUG=b:33450588 TEST=Tested the following on samus-cheets: - Set /proc/fs/kernel/chromiumos/alt_syscall/allow_devmode_syscalls to 1, verify that all CtsSimpleperfTestCases tests pass. - Set /proc/fs/kernel/chromiumos/alt_syscall/allow_devmode_syscalls to 0, verify that those CtsSimpleperfTestCases tests calling perf_event_open fail. Change-Id: Ie94e85f4b48fce4886597f0e49a125b94b36ca18 Signed-off-by: Ben Chan <benchan@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/421087 Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>

login: allow dev-mode only syscalls in containers under dev-mode The alt-syscall kernel module exposes a sysctl entry `/proc/sys/kernel/chromiumos/alt_syscall/allow_devmode_syscalls` for controlling whether certain system calls, which are marked as developer mode only, should be whitelisted for containers. This CL modifies the ui-pre-start job to update that sysctl entry, when exists, under developer mode. containers: support loopback devices Containers that use a filesystem-in-a-file cannot be mounted directly. They have to be added to a loop dev which is then mounted indirectly. Add support for the standard "loop" keyword. This will instruct the container framework to set up the source via a loop device and then mount that instead of the source file. We also have to mount these outside of the userns namespace. The kernel does not allow mounting of any non-pseudo filesystems today inside of a userns. See the FS_USERNS_MOUNT logic in fs/namespace.c. HACK: CHROMIUM: cpufreq: sched: Don't change frequencies when stopped The cpufreq_sched_stop() (called as a result of the CPUFREQ_GOV_STOP selector) wasn't actually causing the "sched" governor to stop changing frequencies. Specifically the cpufreq_sched_thread() kept running after the stop happened and that could keep changing frequencies. The lack of stoppiness in the sched governor is a problem when we have a board relying on "opp-suspend" support. One such board is rk3399-kevin, which relies on the cpu frequency to be less than a certain speed during suspend. In rk3399-kevin's case this is because the suspend process causes certain regulators to drop down to a voltage that cannot support the highest CPU speed. The specific order of calls that shows how this is supposed to work (at least on rk3399-kevin, which uses cpufreq-dt) is: 1. cpufreq_suspend() calls __cpufreq_governor(..., CPUFREQ_GOV_STOP) 2. cpufreq_suspend() calls cpufreq_driver->suspend(...) 3. cpufreq_driver->suspend is cpufreq_generic_suspend() 4. cpufreq_generic_suspend() sets things to the suspend frequency. ...as you can see, if the CPUFREQ_GOV_STOP doesn't actually stop the governor then it's possible we'll end up at a frequency other than the suspend frequency. If it's higher than the suspend frequency we might go boom. A few notes about this implementation: A) This is a "quick and dirty" implementation. I don't actually change any governor logic--I just stop the frequency from changing at times when it shouldn't. Presumably this could mess up the cpufreq accounting slightly if the driver thinks it's running at a different rate than it really is. Hopefully any effects should be short term. B) I don't rely on the "policy->rwsem" for protecting the new "started" member because it appears that cpufreq is not consistent about grabbing that semaphore before calling CPUFREQ_GOV_STOP. Ugh. For old times take, I continue to grab "policy->rwsem" in cpufreq_sched_try_driver_target() where it used to claim "avoid race with cpufreq_sched_stop" even though it's unclear how/why that was supposed to work. It seems safer to leave the semaphore grab in case it had some purpose. BUG=chrome-os-partner:61705 TEST=suspend_stress_test w/ sched governor TEST=Put in test printouts; see cases where we avoided problems Change-Id: I634e0122a10482f44b70d683cf10f58be8306c58 Signed-off-by: Douglas Anderson <dianders@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/426010 Reviewed-by: Sonny Rao <sonnyrao@chromium.org>

init: Allow executing extra commands when inhibited jobs was fired. Upstart is a based on state machine so we sometimes need to do few things, for example firing Upstart events, when a job was inhibited. For example, if job A depends on job B and we only want to inhibit job B (i.e., job A must be executed), then we have to send 'started JOB=B' for Upstart to continue. To support this, common.d/inhibited_jobs/* now supports shell scripts so we can send extra events, or do something else when a job was inhibited. CHROMIUM: LSM: Add support for symlink traversal policy. This change adds functionality to the chromiumos LSM to pin inodes and associate tracking information with them. This allows tracking symlink traversal policy for an inode. Whenever the FS layer follows a link, it calls out to the LSM, which can then check whether a symlink traversal policy has been set on any directory on the path in question. If a policy is set and it specifies that symlink traversal should be blocked, the corresponding FS system call will fail with EPERM. Note that readlink() continues to work, so userspace may resort to resolving symlinks manually if desired. Symlink traversal policy is configured via securityfs. Files in /sys/kernel/security/chromiumos/symlink_policy/ are used to set the symlink traversal policy: * .../allow: Write a path to the file to set the symlink traversal policy for corresponding inode to "allow". * .../block: Write a path to the file to set the symlink traversal policy for corresponding inode to "block". * .../reset: Write a path to clear the symlink traversal policy for the corresponding inode. * .../flush: Write a path to clear symlink traversal policy for the entire file system the corresponding inode belongs to. Note that this may affect paths outside the subtree corresponding to the specified path (e.g. parents, siblings, or parts of the file system not visible in the affected (bind) mount). BUG=chromium:655606 TEST=Set symlink traversal policy and test paths containing symlinks. Change-Id: I844b2aedd7f022d97d28b074d5e98450b66c6992 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/422333 Commit-Ready: Mattias Nissler <mnissler@chromium.org> Tested-by: Mattias Nissler <mnissler@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Dmitry Torokhov <dtor@chromium.org>

UPSTREAM: KEYS: Fix short sprintf buffer in /proc/keys show function This fixes CVE-2016-7042. Fix a short sprintf buffer in proc_keys_show(). If the gcc stack protector is turned on, this can cause a panic due to stack corruption. The problem is that xbuf[] is not big enough to hold a 64-bit timeout rendered as weeks: (gdb) p 0xffffffffffffffffULL/(60*60*24*7) $2 = 30500568904943 That's 14 chars plus NUL, not 11 chars plus NUL. Expand the buffer to 16 chars. I think the unpatched code apparently works if the stack-protector is not enabled because on a 32-bit machine the buffer won't be overflowed and on a 64-bit machine there's a 64-bit aligned pointer at one side and an int that isn't checked again on the other side. The panic incurred looks something like: Kernel panic - not syncing: stack-protector: Kernel stack is corrupted in: ffffffff81352ebe CPU: 0 PID: 1692 Comm: reproducer Not tainted 4.7.2-201.fc24.x86_64 #1 Hardware name: Red Hat KVM, BIOS 0.5.1 01/01/2011 0000000000000086 00000000fbbd2679 ffff8800a044bc00 ffffffff813d941f ffffffff81a28d58 ffff8800a044bc98 ffff8800a044bc88 ffffffff811b2cb6 ffff880000000010 ffff8800a044bc98 ffff8800a044bc30 00000000fbbd2679 Call Trace: [<ffffffff813d941f>] dump_stack+0x63/0x84 [<ffffffff811b2cb6>] panic+0xde/0x22a [<ffffffff81352ebe>] ? proc_keys_show+0x3ce/0x3d0 [<ffffffff8109f7f9>] __stack_chk_fail+0x19/0x30 [<ffffffff81352ebe>] proc_keys_show+0x3ce/0x3d0 [<ffffffff81350410>] ? key_validate+0x50/0x50 [<ffffffff8134db30>] ? key_default_cmp+0x20/0x20 [<ffffffff8126b31c>] seq_read+0x2cc/0x390 [<ffffffff812b6b12>] proc_reg_read+0x42/0x70 [<ffffffff81244fc7>] __vfs_read+0x37/0x150 [<ffffffff81357020>] ? security_file_permission+0xa0/0xc0 [<ffffffff81246156>] vfs_read+0x96/0x130 [<ffffffff81247635>] SyS_read+0x55/0xc0 [<ffffffff817eb872>] entry_SYSCALL_64_fastpath+0x1a/0xa4 Reported-by: Ondrej Kozina <okozina@redhat.com> Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com> Tested-by: Ondrej Kozina <okozina@redhat.com> cc: stable@vger.kernel.org Signed-off-by: James Morris <james.l.morris@oracle.com> (cherry picked from commit 03dab869b7b239c4e013ec82aea22e181e441cfc) BUG=b:33006021, chromium:679485 TEST=kernel compiles Change-Id: Id945e0d89cb53a35eb6add597681fdb3ad045de8 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/413000 Commit-Ready: Andrey Ulanov <andreyu@google.com> Tested-by: Andrey Ulanov <andreyu@google.com> Reviewed-by: Guenter Roeck <groeck@chromium.org> (cherry picked from commit f707658635bb9d9887e213b58da9c263c08a98c8) Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/426095 Commit-Ready: Guenter Roeck <groeck@chromium.org> Tested-by: Guenter Roeck <groeck@chromium.org>

UPSTREAM: KEYS: Fix short sprintf buffer in /proc/keys show function This fixes CVE-2016-7042. Fix a short sprintf buffer in proc_keys_show(). If the gcc stack protector is turned on, this can cause a panic due to stack corruption. The problem is that xbuf[] is not big enough to hold a 64-bit timeout rendered as weeks: (gdb) p 0xffffffffffffffffULL/(60*60*24*7) $2 = 30500568904943 That's 14 chars plus NUL, not 11 chars plus NUL. Expand the buffer to 16 chars. I think the unpatched code apparently works if the stack-protector is not enabled because on a 32-bit machine the buffer won't be overflowed and on a 64-bit machine there's a 64-bit aligned pointer at one side and an int that isn't checked again on the other side.
